strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful practical question: how to make simple feature distillation effective for compact ViTs. Both proposed modifications are straightforward and potentially useful.

Empirical merits: On ImageNet-1K, MSE distillation improves Strategy 1 from its own standalone baseline of 75.41% to 76.61%, and Strategy 2 from 75.54% to 77.15%. These comparisons support a practical benefit beyond the architectural changes alone. Experiments include three teachers and ablations of pooling, projector width, and loss weight.

Presentation: The manuscript is readable, with explicit objectives, clear tables, and supplementary representation plots. It reports major training hyperparameters and hardware. The use of standard image-classification data presents no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—shared-subspace inference: Sections 2.1 and 2.3 incorrectly claim that the 99th percentile of per-image approximation ranks guarantees a single shared projector preserving the desired energy for 99% of images. Each image's SVD can use a different right-singular subspace; even rank-one matrices can collectively span the entire channel space. Equation (1) establishes an image-specific approximation, not the claimed dataset-wide guarantee. A projector fitted across training images and evaluated on held-out images is needed.

Soundness—SEP does not establish encoding capacity: Fourier energy across arbitrarily ordered channels is basis-dependent and does not measure intrinsic dimensionality or necessary student width. For example, X = a e_1^T has rank one, is exactly representable by a one-dimensional bottleneck, and has flat channel-frequency energy for every nonzero token. It therefore exhibits the paper's broad SEP pattern without the claimed capacity bottleneck. Channel permutation or rotation controls and low-rank null examples are missing. Consequently, the central explanation of why feature KD fails is unsupported.

Soundness—linear lifting does not add the claimed expressive capacity: As specified in Section 3.1, the projector followed by a linear classifier computes X_S P W_head, which can be absorbed into a single classifier; GAP also commutes with the linear projector. The lifted representation still has rank at most D_S. Training parameterization may affect optimization, but this does not establish increased intrinsic capacity or a necessity to retain the projector at inference. Any intervening normalization or nonlinearity that changes this argument must be specified.

Experimental attribution: Table 2 lacks ordinary DeiT-Tiny with logit-only KD and, crucially, conventional MSE feature KD using a training-only alignment projector. The claim that MSE fails on the original student is not demonstrated. Strategy 1 also adopts GAP, introducing another difference from the original baseline. The headline improvements include architecture and logit-distillation gains; adding MSE to the corresponding logit-only models contributes only 0.27 and 0.35 percentage points, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. These results do not isolate the proposed mechanism.

Significance and originality: The potentially original contribution is the explanation, but its mathematical foundations are flawed. The methods themselves use familiar projection and width-expansion ideas, with insufficient differentiation from the cited projector and ViT-distillation literature. Comparisons with stronger feature-distillation baselines are absent, and modified-model parameter counts, FLOPs, and latency are unreported. Generality is tested with only one student and dataset; in Table 6, Strategy 2 with DeiT-Small improves over its own standalone baseline by just 0.12–0.19 points.

Reproducibility and limitations: The manuscript does not adequately specify the width-transition implementation for the final block, exact teacher checkpoints and feature-extraction locations, distillation temperature, or implementation details of SpectralKD. No code availability statement or repeated-seed results are provided. Limitations are not substantively discussed, while claims that the experiments 'confirm' a fundamental architectural bottleneck exceed the evidence. These issues, together with the central analytical errors, prevent acceptance despite the promising empirical gains.

strengths: Significance: Improving simple feature distillation for compact ViTs is a useful objective. The reported ImageNet-1K results show practical promise: MSE-only distillation reaches 76.61% and 77.15%, compared with the corresponding modified students’ standalone accuracies of 75.41% and 75.54%.

Empirical coverage: The paper includes representation diagnostics across six architectures, experiments with three teachers, and ablations on pooling, projector width, and loss weight. Reporting standalone architectural improvements helps distinguish some architectural benefits from distillation benefits.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable, with explicit loss equations and clearly organized tables. The two proposed modifications are conceptually simple.
Originality: Connecting representation diagnostics to final-block architecture and projector placement is a potentially useful research direction, even though the individual components are familiar.
weaknesses: Soundness—incorrect shared-subspace inference: Sections 2.1 and 2.3 explicitly claim that the 99th percentile of per-image effective ranks guarantees a single shared projector preserving the target energy for 99% of images. This does not follow: each image’s SVD can have a different right-singular subspace. Even rank-one matrices can collectively span the entire channel space. Equation (1) establishes an optimal factorization for an individual matrix, not one projector shared across inputs. Dataset-level subspace estimation and held-out reconstruction measurements are needed to establish this central premise.

Soundness—SEP does not establish encoding capacity: Fourier energy along arbitrarily ordered feature channels is basis-dependent and does not measure intrinsic dimensionality or the minimum width needed for reconstruction. For example, tokens of the form x_t = a_t v can have broad Fourier energy when v does, while requiring only one scalar and a fixed linear decoder. Thus, low rank and broad SEP are entirely compatible without the proposed capacity obstacle. Channel-permutation controls, low-rank synthetic controls, and evidence connecting SEP to distillation difficulty are missing.

Soundness—linear lifting does not supply the claimed representational capacity: X_S P still has rank at most D_S. Furthermore, for the inference architecture described in Section 3.1, a linear projector followed by a linear classifier can be absorbed into a single classifier, including with GAP or CLS selection. Retaining this factorization may affect training and optimization, but it does not establish increased inference expressivity or the necessity of retaining the projector. If an intervening normalization changes this argument, its placement must be specified and ablated.

Experimental attribution: Table 2 lacks the decisive conventional baseline: normalized MSE with a training-only projector, under matched pooling and training settings. The text claims that MSE fails on the original student, but reports only SpectralKD for that configuration. An original-student logit-only baseline is also absent. Relative to each modified model’s logit-only result, adding MSE improves accuracy by 0.27 and 0.35 percentage points; the headline gains of approximately three points therefore cannot be attributed primarily to feature distillation. The change to GAP in Strategy 1 further requires a matched original-student GAP control.

Significance and generality are overstated: Distillation is evaluated on one dataset and one student architecture, with all teachers having width 384. In Table 6, Strategy 2 with DeiT-Small improves only 0.12–0.19 points over its own 75.54% standalone baseline, and DeiT3-Small with MSE improves 0.28 points. Without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, consistent reactivation across teachers is not established. Modified-model parameter counts, FLOPs, and latency are also missing, limiting assessment of the compression trade-off.

Originality and comparative evaluation: The methods use established ingredients—linear feature adapters, normalized feature matching, and architectural widening. Their main distinguishing contribution is therefore the explanatory analysis, whose central inferences are unsupported. Although relevant projector and ViT-distillation methods are cited, the experiments do not establish competitiveness against those approaches under matched conditions.

Reproducibility and limitations: The manuscript provides useful optimizer settings but leaves important implementation choices unclear, including the transition into the widened block, classifier-path normalization, exact teacher checkpoints, distillation temperature, and feature/token selection. No executable implementation or seed variability is supplied. The width ablation claims weaker MSE robustness at width 448 without reporting those MSE results. The conclusion repeatedly treats the mechanism as confirmed without discussing these alternative explanations and evidential limits. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by technical and evidential weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful practical question: how to make feature distillation effective for compact ViTs using simple architectural changes and losses. Both proposed strategies are straightforward to implement.

Empirical merits: The CaiT-S24 experiments show meaningful gains over architecture-matched standalone students. MSE-only distillation improves Strategy 1 from 75.41% to 76.61% and Strategy 2 from 75.54% to 77.15%. Combining feature and logit distillation reaches 78.23%. These results warrant further investigation independently of the proposed explanation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is readable, provides explicit objectives and substantial training details, and includes ablations on pooling, projector width, loss weight, and teacher choice. The representation diagnostics cover several architectures, with supplementary distributions and variability plots.
weaknesses: Soundness—shared-subspace inference: Sections 2.1 and 2.3 incorrectly claim that the 99th percentile of per-image effective ranks guarantees a single shared projector preserving the target energy for 99% of images. Equation (1) optimizes a projector separately for each feature matrix; different images can have different right-singular subspaces. Even rank-one matrices can collectively span the entire channel space. A dataset-level subspace analysis and held-out reconstruction with a fixed projector are needed. This error undermines the foundational claim of globally shared low-dimensional structure.

Soundness—SEP does not establish required capacity: Fourier energy across arbitrarily ordered channels is basis-dependent and does not measure intrinsic dimensionality or the minimum width needed to reproduce a representation. For example, tokens of the form x_t = a_t v can have broadly distributed Fourier energy while admitting an exact one-dimensional encoding and linear decoder. Thus, low rank and broad SEP are compatible without any additional capacity bottleneck. Channel-permutation controls, low-rank synthetic controls, and direct reconstruction experiments are missing; the central encoding-mismatch explanation is not established.

Soundness—linear lifting interpretation: As specified in Section 3.1, the projector followed by a linear classifier can be composed into a single classifier: X_S P W_head = X_S W_eff. This also holds with the described GAP or CLS selection. The projector does not increase the representation's rank beyond the student width, and retaining it at inference is not mathematically necessary under this architecture. Training parameterization or auxiliary supervision could explain improvements, but the claimed increase in necessary encoding capacity requires a different argument. Any intervening nonlinear normalization must be specified explicitly.

Experimental attribution: Table 2 omits both ordinary MSE distillation with a training-only alignment projector and logit-only distillation on the original student. These are essential controls for the claimed failure and reactivation of simple feature KD. The headline gains also include architectural changes and logit supervision: adding MSE over architecture-matched SoftKD improves accuracy by only 0.27 and 0.35 percentage points. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied. Strategy 1 additionally adopts GAP, leaving pooling as a potential confound in comparisons with the original baseline.

Significance and generality: All distillation experiments use one student and one dataset, and all tested teachers have width 384. Table 6 provides weaker support than its discussion suggests: Strategy 2 with DeiT-Small MSE reaches 75.66%, only 0.12 points above its 75.54% standalone baseline. Modified-model parameter counts, FLOPs, latency, and compute-matched architectural controls are absent, limiting the practical compression claim.

Originality and positioning: The potentially distinctive contribution is the proposed explanatory account, but that account has the soundness problems above. Linear alignment projectors and width changes alone offer limited demonstrated methodological novelty. The manuscript cites projector-focused work, ViTKD, manifold distillation, and ScaleKD without sufficiently distinguishing its mechanism or providing relevant controlled comparisons.

Reproducibility and limitations: Important implementation details remain unclear, including the transition into the widened final block, exact teacher checkpoints and feature extraction points, distillation temperature, and implementation of unequal-width SpectralKD. The manuscript also does not adequately acknowledge the basis dependence of SEP, per-image versus dataset-level rank distinction, or limited causal evidence. I identify no specific material ethical concern; the decisive barriers to acceptance are technical and evidential.

strengths: Soundness: The distinction between per-image compressibility and reconstruction within a shared channel subspace is useful and mathematically well motivated. For CaiT-S24, the reported 99th-percentile dimensions for 95% energy are 61 under per-image SVD versus 302 under shared PCA. Table 1 and Appendix B extend this observation across supervised, self-supervised, and multimodal models.

Significance: The architectural modifications are simple and produce promising ImageNet results. Relative to their own standalone baselines, MSE distillation improves Lift from 75.41% to 76.61% and WideLast from 75.54% to 77.15% with CaiT-S24. These improvements establish practical merit independently of the proposed explanation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript clearly defines its SVD/PCA diagnostics, acknowledges the token-count rank ceiling, explains the use of uncentered second moments, and provides extensive diagnostic plots. Optimizer, training schedule, batch size, and hardware are reported, and supplementary code and raw data are stated to be available.

Limitations and ethics: The conclusion appropriately identifies intermediate-layer analysis and additional downstream tasks as future work. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the described standard image-classification experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—SEP does not establish the claimed capacity requirement. Sections 2.3–2.6 interpret broad Fourier energy across channel indices as evidence that a token requires near-teacher representation width. Channel ordering has no established frequency semantics, and this statistic depends on the coordinate basis. A one-dimensional family x = a e1 already has energy across all DFT frequencies while admitting exact scalar encoding and linear decoding. Thus high SEP bandwidth can coexist with extremely low intrinsic capacity requirements. Random-basis, permutation, and low-rank controls are needed; the reported curves do not support an architecture-invariant encoding law with the claimed consequences.

Soundness—Lift does not increase representational dimension as claimed. Equation (11), X_hat = XS P, still confines every output to the same subspace of dimension at most DS. Moreover, with the described linear classifier and either GAP or CLS selection, P can be absorbed into the classifier: XS P Whead = XS W_eff. Retaining P therefore does not expand the classification function class or remove a rank bottleneck. Optimization or regularization effects could explain gains, but Sections 3.1 and 4.5 incorrectly treat them as evidence of increased endpoint capacity.

Experimental attribution: Table 2 omits the original student's SoftKD baseline and a conventional MSE-with-projector baseline, despite claiming that MSE fails on the original student. Lift also uses GAP in the main experiments, requiring controls that independently vary pooling, projector placement, and classifier parameterization. The headline improvements of 2.67–3.37 points combine architectural changes, logit KD, and feature KD; feature KD adds only about 0.3–0.35 points over the corresponding SoftKD variants. These comparisons do not isolate the proposed failure mechanism.

Evidence and uncertainty: All distillation experiments use one student and one dataset, and the additional teachers retain the same 384-channel width. Table 6 compares against the original 74.86% baseline, although WideLast already achieves 75.54% without distillation; its DeiT-Small results therefore improve by only 0.12–0.19 points. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. Teacher reconstruction losses, student geometry before and after modification, and controlled width-dependent predictions are also absent, leaving the connection between reconstruction limits and classification gains unverified.

Originality and significance: The strongest potentially original contribution is the explanatory synthesis, but its SEP and Lift arguments are unsupported. Linear projection and localized widening are modest architectural changes, and the paper does not empirically distinguish their contribution from the alignment methods discussed in Appendix A. Modified-model parameter counts, FLOPs, latency, and comparisons against equally costly capacity increases are missing, limiting assessment of the compression benefit.

Reproducibility: The manuscript does not adequately specify the narrow-to-wide transition inside WideLast, its attention configuration, exact feature extraction and normalization, or complete logit-distillation settings. The implementation of unequal-width SpectralKD comparisons is also insufficiently described. Although supplementary code is announced, it was not available in the supplied material for verification. Overall, the useful empirical observations do not compensate for the unresolved central soundness issues.

strengths: Soundness: The distinction between per-image compressibility and reconstruction within a shared linear subspace is valid and useful. For CaiT-S24, Figure 1 reports 99th-percentile dimensions of 61 versus 302 for preserving 95% energy. Table 1 and Appendix B extend this observation across multiple architectures and training regimes.

Significance: The architectural variants yield promising ImageNet-1K results. Relative to their own standalone baselines, MSE distillation improves Lift from 75.41% to 76.61% and WideLast from 75.54% to 77.15%. These are potentially useful practical findings even without the proposed explanation.

Presentation and originality: The manuscript clearly defines its SVD and uncentered PCA diagnostics, acknowledges the token-count rank ceiling, and provides extensive supporting plots. Comparing sample-specific and shared-subspace reconstruction offers a useful empirical perspective on distillation.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper provides major training settings and states that code and raw data accompany the submission, although those materials were not available in the supplied manuscript. The conclusion identifies several scope limitations, and the described research raises no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—SEP does not establish the claimed capacity requirement. Sections 2.3–2.6 interpret broad Fourier energy across channel indices as evidence that tokens require near-teacher representational width. Channel indices have no established spatial or frequency ordering, and this diagnostic depends on the coordinate basis. For example, tokens x_t = a_t v occupy a fixed one-dimensional subspace even if v has a broad Fourier spectrum; a one-dimensional representation and fixed linear decoder reproduce them exactly. Thus broad SEP does not establish an additional bottleneck beyond subspace dimension. Channel-permutation, random-feature, and synthetic low-rank controls are needed before describing this as an architecture-invariant encoding law.

Soundness—Lift does not increase representational capacity as claimed. Equation (11) gives X_hat = X_S P, whose rows remain in a fixed subspace of dimension at most D_S. Moreover, with the stated linear classifier and either GAP or CLS selection, P can be absorbed into the classifier: W_effective = P W_head. Retaining P therefore does not enlarge the inference function class relative to an unrestricted linear head on the same student features. Factorization can affect optimization and the auxiliary loss, but the manuscript attributes gains to additional endpoint capacity without establishing that mechanism.

Experimental attribution is inadequate. Table 2 omits ordinary-student SoftKD, MSE with a conventional training-only projector, and SoftKD plus feature-loss controls. Lift also adopts GAP, so the headline comparison against 74.86% mixes several changes. Adding feature KD to SoftKD improves Lift by only 0.30 percentage points and WideLast by 0.35 points, much less than the headline improvements. Matched pooling and projector controls, together with repeated runs, are necessary to isolate the proposed contribution.

The experiments do not directly validate the proposed failure mechanism. Teacher reconstruction energy is not shown to predict student accuracy or the benefit of either intervention. There are no measurements demonstrating that WideLast reduces the relevant reconstruction residual or better tracks input-dependent subspaces. Table 4 also does not establish a special benefit from matching teacher width: standalone accuracy peaks at 320 channels, while SpectralKD accuracy peaks at 448. The discussion invokes poorer MSE robustness at 448 without reporting those results.

Significance and originality remain insufficiently established. Distillation experiments use one student, one dataset, and exclusively 384-channel teachers. The broad representation survey does not establish equally broad intervention effectiveness. Lift and WideLast are simple architectural changes whose novelty rests substantially on the unsupported capacity explanation. Comparisons with the alignment methods discussed in Appendix A, and parameter/FLOP/latency measurements for the modified students, are missing; consequently, their accuracy–efficiency value for compression is unclear.

Reproducibility and presentation need substantive clarification. The manuscript does not specify how the narrow representation enters WideLast's wider block, including its residual path, or fully specify feature normalization, loss reduction, logit temperature, and loss weights for the main configurations. No seed variability is reported. Appendix C also reports effective dimensions as b_alpha D although Equation (10) defines bandwidth using D-prime unique Fourier bins. These ambiguities accompany repeated causal claims stronger than the evidence supports. Overall, the useful geometric observations and accuracy gains do not compensate for the unresolved flaws in the central explanation.

strengths: Soundness: The distinction between per-image low rank and dataset-wide linear compressibility is valid and well illustrated. For CaiT-S24, Figure 1 reports 99th-percentile dimensions of 61 versus 302 for retaining 95% energy. Table 1 and Appendix B extend this useful observation across supervised, self-supervised, and multimodal models.

Significance: The proposed modifications are simple and produce promising ImageNet-1K results. Table 2 reports 77.53% and 78.23% accuracy for Lift and WideLast, compared with 74.86% for the original student. Feature-only and teacher-free experiments provide useful evidence beyond the strongest combined-distillation configuration.

Presentation and originality: The manuscript clearly organizes the geometric diagnostics, architectural interventions, and ablations. Connecting shared-subspace reconstruction constraints to the distillation interface is a useful interpretive contribution, even though linear projectors and width changes are established tools.

Reproducibility and ethics: The manuscript specifies major training settings, hardware, and model sources, and states that code and raw data accompany the submission. It acknowledges untested downstream settings and intermediate-layer extensions. The described research raises no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—SEP does not establish the claimed capacity requirement. Sections 2.3–2.6 interpret broad Fourier energy across channel indices as evidence that tokens require near-teacher width. Channel order has no justified spatial or frequency structure, and SEP is basis dependent. For example, tokens x_t = a_t v can have broad Fourier spectra for a fixed vector v while being exactly representable with one scalar and a fixed linear decoder. Thus, high SEP bandwidth can coexist with a one-dimensional shared representation. Permutation, random-basis, and synthetic low-rank controls are needed; the current evidence does not support the central 'encoding law' interpretation.

Soundness—Lift does not increase representational capacity as claimed. Equation 11 gives X_S P, whose rank remains at most D_S and whose rows remain in a fixed subspace of dimension at most D_S. Moreover, under the stated linear classifier and GAP or CLS readout, P can be absorbed into the classifier as P W_head. Retaining it at inference therefore does not enlarge the classifier's function class. Training benefits could arise from optimization, regularization, or coupling the classifier to the distillation projection, but they do not demonstrate removal of a capacity bottleneck.

Experimental attribution is insufficient. Table 2 omits the original student's SoftKD-only result and a conventional MSE baseline with a training-time alignment projector, despite claiming that original-student MSE fails. Lift also adopts GAP, without a matched GAP baseline lacking Lift. Relative to each modified model's SoftKD result, the best combined feature loss adds only 0.30 points for Lift and 0.35 for WideLast; the headline gains of 2.67 and 3.37 points cannot be attributed to reactivated feature KD alone.

The geometric observations are not causally connected to distillation outcomes. The paper does not measure whether the modifications reduce feature reconstruction error, approach the shared-PCA bound, or produce input-dependent subspaces as proposed. Preserving 95% or 99% of raw feature energy is also not shown to be necessary for classification. WideLast's additional nonlinear capacity is plausible, but accuracy improvements alone do not validate the proposed failure mechanism.

Significance and originality remain insufficiently established experimentally. Distillation is evaluated with one student on one dataset, and the additional teachers all have width 384. There are no direct comparisons with the relevant alignment methods discussed in Appendix A or parameter/FLOP-matched widening controls. Modified-model parameter counts, FLOPs, and latency are absent, preventing assessment of the claimed compression trade-off. In Table 6, WideLast with DeiT-Small improves only 0.12–0.19 points over its own 75.54% standalone baseline.

Reproducibility and uncertainty need improvement. No repeated-seed results or confidence intervals support the small incremental gains. The manuscript leaves the narrow-to-wide transition in WideLast, precise feature extraction and normalization, and several loss settings underspecified. It states that supplementary code exists, but that material was not available in the supplied review materials. The limitations discussion identifies useful future directions but does not address the central basis-dependence and linear-capacity issues. These unresolved soundness problems outweigh the promising empirical results.
